item.title: And, bhikkhus, a true person reflects: 'It is not because of being a forest-dweller that the states of greed come to be abandoned, or the…
item.description:
And, bhikkhus, a true person reflects: 'It is not because of being a forest-dweller that the states of greed come to be abandoned, or the states of hatred, or the states of delusion. If a person who has gone forth is not a forest-dweller, yet practices in accordance with the Dhamma and in conformity with the Dhamma, practices rightly, practices in conformity with the Dhamma, then he is honored and praised here.' Having taken the path as the essential, he does not praise himself or disparage others because of his own being a forest-dweller. Thus, bhikkhus, is the true person's quality.

item.title: Fear, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. Suffering, bhikkhus, is a companion of sensual pleasures. Illness, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. A…
item.description:
Fear, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. Suffering, bhikkhus, is a companion of sensual pleasures. Illness, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. A boil, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. Clinging, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. A swamp, bhikkhus, is a designation for sensual pleasures. And, bhikkhus, why is fear a designation for sensual pleasures? Bhikkhus, being infatuated by sensual desire, bound by sensual desire, one does not escape from fear in this very life, nor does one escape from fear in the hereafter. Therefore, fear is a designation for sensual pleasures.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.23

item.title: Bhikkhus, I sought the gratification in the world. Whatever gratification there is in the world, I found it. To whatever extent gratification exists in the…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, I sought the gratification in the world. Whatever gratification there is in the world, I found it. To whatever extent gratification exists in the world, I have seen it well with wisdom. Bhikkhus, I sought the danger in the world. Whatever danger there is in the world, I found it. To whatever extent danger exists in the world, I have seen it well with wisdom. Bhikkhus, I sought the escape from the world. Whatever escape there is from the world, I found it. To whatever extent escape exists from the world, I have seen it well with wisdom.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.104

item.title: Bhikkhus, it is through attachment that one is not liberated. Through attachment to form, bhikkhus, consciousness, having a foothold, becomes established. With form as object,…
item.description:
Bhikkhus, it is through attachment that one is not liberated. Through attachment to form, bhikkhus, consciousness, having a foothold, becomes established. With form as object, with form as support, seeking delight, it comes to growth, increase, and expansion. Through attachment to feeling ... through attachment to perception ... through attachment to formations, bhikkhus, consciousness, having a foothold, becomes established. With formations as object, with formations as support, seeking delight, it comes to growth, increase, and expansion. Bhikkhus, one who says: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will describe the coming and going, the passing away and arising, the growth, increase, and expansion of consciousness' — that is impossible. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the form element, with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, and the support of consciousness does not exist. Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the feeling element ... for the perception element ... for the formation element ... Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu has abandoned lust for the consciousness element, with the abandonment of lust, the basis is cut off, and the support of consciousness does not exist. Without that support, consciousness does not grow, does not form, is liberated. Through liberation, it is steady. Through steadiness, it is content. Through contentment, it is not distressed. Not distressed, he personally attains Nibbāna. He understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no further existence after this life.'

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.53

item.title: In whatever families, bhikkhus, the children at home honor their mother and father, those families are considered equal to Brahmā. In whatever families, bhikkhus, the…
item.description:
In whatever families, bhikkhus, the children at home honor their mother and father, those families are considered equal to Brahmā. In whatever families, bhikkhus, the children at home honor their mother and father, those families are considered like the ancient teachers. In whatever families, bhikkhus, the children at home honor their mother and father, those families are considered worthy of offerings.

item.description:
Thus, Ambattha, you and your teacher are not true ascetics, you do not live the life of an ascetic. Ambattha, if there is anything you doubt or are uncertain about regarding me, ask me and I will answer.

item.title: If a bhikkhu possesses six qualities, bhikkhus, whether by day or by night, a decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth. What…
item.description:
If a bhikkhu possesses six qualities, bhikkhus, whether by day or by night, a decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth. What six? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has great desires, is discontented, is not satisfied with any kind of basic necessities such as robes, almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites; he has no faith, is immoral, is lazy, has forgetful mindfulness, and has evil wisdom.

item.title: And, Aggivessana, what is the trained body and what is the trained mind? Here, Aggivessana, a learned noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling. Experiencing a…
item.description:
And, Aggivessana, what is the trained body and what is the trained mind? Here, Aggivessana, a learned noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling. Experiencing a pleasant feeling, he is not attached to that pleasant feeling, does not fall into attachment to it. If that pleasant feeling ceases, with the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Experiencing that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, grieve, lament, beat his breast, or become confused. Aggivessana, that pleasant feeling that arose for that person does not invade his mind and does not remain — because the body is trained. That painful feeling that arose for that person does not invade his mind and does not remain — because the mind is trained. Aggivessana, in whatever person, both ways, a pleasant feeling arises, does not invade the mind and does not remain — because the body is trained; a painful feeling arises, does not invade the mind and does not remain — because the mind is trained. Thus, Aggivessana, that person is one with a trained body and a trained mind.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 36 – Mahāsaccakasutta

item.title: - Just as, bhikkhus, a stick thrown up into the sky sometimes falls on its base, sometimes in the middle, sometimes on its tip. So…
item.description:
- Just as, bhikkhus, a stick thrown up into the sky sometimes falls on its base, sometimes in the middle, sometimes on its tip. So too, bhikkhus, beings shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving, wandering and roaming on, sometimes go from this world to another world, sometimes from another world to this world. Why is that? Because they do not see the Four Noble Truths. What four? The Noble Truth of Suffering ... the Noble Truth of the Path leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 56.33
